script:
Roth or traditional 401k? Here's exactly how to choose.
And it really comes down to one thing, your tax bracket.
Both are the same 401k, the only difference is when the IRS gets paid.
Traditional, your money goes in before taxes, and you pay income tax when you pull it out.
Roth, you pay the tax today, and once you're 59 and a half and the account's been open five years, it all comes out tax free.
Here's the math.
Let's say you're in the 22% bracket and you've got $10,000 of salary to invest.
Traditional, the full $10,000 goes in.
Roth, you pay $2,200 in tax first, so $7,800 goes in.
Now let's say your investments quadruple by the time you retire.
Traditional is sitting at $40,000, Roth is at $31,200.
But the traditional still owes tax.
If you're still in the 22% bracket in retirement, you keep $31,200.
The exact same number. It's a tie.
Which is crazy, because people argue about this all day.
But if you drop to the 12% bracket in retirement, traditional leaves you with $35,200.
That's $4,000 more than the Roth.
And if you climb to the 24% bracket, you keep $30,400, and the Roth wins.
So here are the questions that decide it for you.
One, what bracket are you in today?
Two, will you be in a higher or lower bracket when you retire?
Higher later, lean Roth. Lower later, lean traditional.
Three, be honest, will you actually invest the tax savings from the traditional, or just spend it?
If you're gonna spend it, the Roth forces you to save it.
And if you have no idea, you don't have to pick.
You can split your contributions between both, up to $25,500 total for 2027.
This is simplified math, your real tax return has more moving parts, so do your own research.
Are you Roth or traditional? Let me know down below.
And as always, if you're looking to grow your net worth, follow me.

sources.supports: Roth 401(k) contributions are after-tax and traditional are before-tax; traditional withdrawals are subject to income tax; Roth withdrawals of contributions and earnings are untaxed once the account is held at least 5 years and you are 59½ or older; you can split deferrals between Roth and pre-tax under one combined limit
Roth and pre-tax 401(k) contributions can be made in the same year in any proportion the plan permits; a qualified Roth distribution requires five years plus age 59½
The 401(k) employee contribution limit is $25,500 for 2027
The 12%, 22% and 24% federal brackets exist as used in the worked example (the dollar figures are my own arithmetic on a hypothetical $10,000 that quadruples)

Higher marginal rate in retirement favors Roth and lower favors traditional; the same rate now and later gives the same result; traditional tax savings only help if you invest rather than spend them, and Roth removes that temptation; splitting between both is an option
